subject: Chemistry
title: Why Oil and Water Don't Mix
description: A quick win: understand Why Oil and Water Don't Mix.

hook.text: Pour oil into water and they separate instantly. No amount of stirring will keep them mixed.

buildup.text: Water molecules are polar—they have a positive end and a negative end. They attract each other tightly.

discovery.text: Oil molecules are nonpolar. They can't form hydrogen bonds with water, so water pushes them away.

twist.text: Soap fixes this. Its molecules have a polar head that grabs water and a nonpolar tail that grabs oil.

climax.text: Emulsifiers in mayonnaise, milk, and salad dressing do the same job—bridging oil and water.

punchline.text: Polar meets nonpolar: rejection. Add soap and they get along.

quiz.question: Why don't oil and water mix?
options: Oil is nonpolar and can't form hydrogen bonds with polar water
Oil molecules are too large to fit between water molecules

details.summary: Oil and water do not mix because water molecules are polar and form hydrogen bonds with each other, while oil molecules are nonpolar. The thermodynamic cost of disrupting water's hydrogen bond network to accommodate oil molecules is too high, so the two liquids separate into distinct layers.
details.whyItMatters: The immiscibility of oil and water is central to cooking, cleaning, biology, and industrial chemistry. It underpins emulsification, cell membrane structure, and pollution cleanup.
takeaways: Water is polar and oil is nonpolar, preventing molecular mixing
The hydrophobic effect drives oil molecules to cluster together
Emulsifiers bridge this gap by having both polar and nonpolar regions

faq.question: Is the separation of oil and water about attraction or repulsion?
faq.answer: It is primarily about water's strong attraction to itself rather than repulsion of oil. Water molecules form an extensive hydrogen bond network that is energetically costly to disrupt. Oil molecules are excluded not because water repels them, but because water prefers bonding with itself.

faq.question: How do emulsifiers like lecithin make oil and water mix?
faq.answer: Emulsifiers have a polar end that dissolves in water and a nonpolar end that dissolves in oil. They sit at the interface between droplets and the surrounding liquid, reducing surface tension and preventing separated droplets from merging back together. Mayonnaise is a classic emulsion.
